source_text: Qualia autem sunt, fratres dilectissimi, orationis dominicae sacramenta, quam multa, quam magna, breuiter in sermone collecta sed in uirtute spiritaliter copiosa, ut nihil omnino praetermissum sit quod non in precibus adque orationibus nostris caelestis doctrinae conpendio conprehendatur! sic, ait, adorate: pater noster, qui es in caelis. homo nouus, renatus et Deo suo per eius gratiam restitutus pater primo in loco dicit, quia filius esse iam coepit. in sua, inquit, propria uenitet sui eum non receperunt. quotquot eum receperunt dedit illis potestatem ut filii Dei fierent, qui credunt in nomine eius.. qui ergo credidit in nomine eius et factus est Dei filius, hinc debet incipere, ut et gratias agat et profiteatur se Dei filium, dum nominat patrem sibi esse in caelis Deum, contestetur quoque inter prima statim natiuitatis suae uerba renuntiasse se terreno et carnali patri et patrem solum nosse se et habere coepisse qui sit in caelis, sicut scriptum est: qui dicunt patri et matri: non noui te, et filios suos non agnouerunt, hi custodierunt praecepta tua et testamentum tuum seruauerunt. item Dominus in euangelio suo praecepit ne uocemus nobis patrem in terra, quod scilicet nobis unus pater qui est in caelis. et discipulo qui mentionem defuncti patris fecerat respondit: sine mortui mortuos suos sepeliant. dixerat enim patrem suum mortuum, cum sit credentium pater uiuus.
thought_title: The new birth teaches us to call God Father
orientation: Cyprian has just begun his treatise and now opens his explanation of the Lord's Prayer by showing that the address 'our Father' belongs only to those reborn as God's children.
pass_a_gloss: But of what kind are, most beloved brothers, the mysteries of the Lord's Prayer, how many, how great, briefly gathered in speech but spiritually rich in power, so that nothing at all has been passed over that is not comprehended in the compendium of heavenly teaching in our prayers and petitions! Thus, he says, pray: our Father, who are in heaven. The new man, reborn and restored to his God through his grace, says Father in the first place, because he has already begun to be a son. He came into his own, it says, and his own did not receive him. As many as received him, he gave them power to become children of God, to those who believe in his name. Therefore he who has believed in his name and has been made a child of God ought to begin from this, that he both give thanks and profess himself a child of God, while he names God as Father to himself in heaven, let him also bear witness among the first words immediately of his new birth that he has renounced the earthly and fleshly father and has begun to know and have as father only him who is in heaven, as it is written: those who say to father and mother: I have not known you, and have not acknowledged their sons, these have kept your precepts and have preserved your covenant. Likewise the Lord in his gospel commanded that we should not call a father for ourselves on earth, because of course there is for us one Father who is in heaven. And to the disciple who had made mention of his dead father he answered: let the dead bury their own dead. For he had said that his father was dead, although the Father of believers is living.

choices.why: Cyprian uses sacramentum for the hidden spiritual realities of the prayer, not a liturgical rite here.
Keeps the Pauline sense of the reborn person as a new creation.
Fixed glossary rendering for the opening address of the Lord's Prayer.
Fixed glossary rendering for Christians as God's children through rebirth.
Preserves the contrast between earthly and heavenly fatherhood that Cyprian draws.

choices.english: the Father of believers is living
choices.why: Keeps the present tense force of 'uiuus' as a predicate adjective.

pass_b_english: What mysteries the Lord's Prayer contains, dearly beloved brothers—how many, how great! They are gathered briefly in words, yet spiritually rich in power, so that nothing at all is left out that is not included in this summary of heavenly teaching for our prayers and petitions. "Pray like this," he says: "Our Father, who are in heaven" (Matthew 6:9). The new man, reborn and restored to his God through his grace, says "Father" first of all, because he has now begun to be a son. "He came to his own," he says, "and his own did not receive him. But to all who received him he gave power to become children of God, to those who believe in his name" (John 1:11-12). So whoever has believed in his name and become a child of God must begin from this point: he must give thanks and confess that he is God's child, and when he names God as his Father in heaven, he must also bear witness in the very first words of his new birth that he has renounced the earthly and fleshly father and has begun to know and have only the Father who is in heaven. As it is written: "They who say to their father and mother, 'I do not know you,' and do not acknowledge their own children—these have kept your precepts and preserved your covenant" (Deuteronomy 33:9). Likewise the Lord commanded in his gospel that we should call no one on earth our father, because there is one Father for us, who is in heaven (Matthew 23:9). And to the disciple who mentioned his dead father, he answered: "Let the dead bury their own dead" (Matthew 8:22). For the disciple had said his father was dead, but the Father of believers is living.

last_rejected.quote: he must also bear witness in the very first words of his new birth that he has renounced the earthly and fleshly father and has begun to know and have only the Father who is in heaven
last_rejected.source_quote: contestetur quoque inter prima statim natiuitatis suae uerba renuntiasse se terreno et carnali patri et patrem solum nosse se et habere coepisse qui sit in caelis
last_rejected.why: The English says he renounced 'the earthly and fleshly father' (singular, one father). The Latin says he renounced an earthly and fleshly father (patri, dative singular but indefinite), and begun to know and have only the Father in heaven.
last_rejected.fix: he must also bear witness in the very first words of his new birth that he has renounced an earthly and fleshly father and has begun to know and have only the Father who is in heaven
last_rejected.ruling: Latin 'patri' dative singular refers to one's own earthly father; English 'the' is normal definite article for generic singular reference, not a mistranslation.

last_rejected.quote: "He came to his own," he says
last_rejected.why: The 'he says' attributes John 1:11 to Christ, but source 'inquit' refers to John the evangelist, not Christ.
last_rejected.fix: "He came to his own," says the evangelist, "and his own did not receive him."
last_rejected.ruling: 'inquit' simply introduces the quotation; English 'he says' does not force attribution to Christ rather than the evangelist.

last_rejected.quote: because there is one Father for us
last_rejected.source_quote: quod scilicet nobis unus pater qui est in caelis
last_rejected.why: 'quod scilicet' means 'since obviously/clearly,' not 'because'; and Latin lacks 'there is.'
last_rejected.fix: since clearly we have one Father, who is in heaven
last_rejected.ruling: 'quod scilicet' = 'because clearly'; 'there is' is implicit in Latin. Both renderings are within normal range.

last_rejected.quote: For the disciple had said his father was dead
last_rejected.source_quote: dixerat enim patrem suum mortuum, cum sit credentium pater uiuus
last_rejected.why: The contrast is missing: 'cum sit credentium pater uiuus' = 'while the Father of believers is living.'
last_rejected.fix: For he had called his father dead, while the Father of believers is living.
last_rejected.ruling: English 'but the Father of believers is living' renders the contrast of 'cum sit' adequately; 'but' conveys the concessive sense.
